rules.title: Spacious density
rules.description: Use a spacious layout density with more whitespace.
rules.rationale: Western homepages in the sample show about a third of the visual density of Chinese ones and fewer content blocks (2026 study). NN/G found that foreign participants were less annoyed by problems on simple sites than on complex ones. Raising whitespace moves a dense page toward the sparser convention without removing content. It fires only when the measured page is denser than the midpoint between the two sample means, so pages that are already sparse are left alone.

evidence.summary: Measured lower visual density and fewer content blocks on Western homepages; weak supporting user evidence.

sources.locator: Section 2.2 table: visual density 12.87 vs 38.21 per 1,000 px; main content blocks 3.14 vs 5.91
sources.supports: Lower density and fewer blocks on Western homepages

sources.locator: Section 'Yes, Chinese Sites Are Often Complex': foreign participants less likely to be annoyed by usability issues on simple sites than on complex ones (n=6 expatriates)
sources.supports: Weak support: tolerance of simple sites among non-Chinese participants

gaps: Sample is institutional (municipal) homepages; commercial sites are not covered.
NN/G does not report a general Western preference for simplicity; its non-Chinese participants were 6 expatriates living in China.
Search-results and article pages are extrapolations from homepages.

Delta-based: the density threshold (25.54) is the midpoint of two sample means from a study of municipal homepages. It is provisional and compared against our own metric definition, whose scale may differ from the study's. Replace with own measurements (A2).

limits: Tendency from research, not a universal rule; varies by site and sector.
Only spacing changes; content must not be hidden.
Does nothing on pages already at or below the threshold; also does nothing if the page could not be measured.

rules.title: Airy spacing scale
rules.rationale: Literature review reports more white space on Western sites; white space acts as a structural element in the Western model (doc 01 section 3.3).

evidence.summary: Review of 17 studies reports more white space on Western sites.

sources.locator: Section 2.1: Western sites have more white space
sources.supports: More white space on Western sites

sources.locator: Section 3.3: white space is a structural element in the West
sources.supports: Interpretation of the role of white space

gaps: Methods and definitions of white space differ across the reviewed studies.
No test of whether adding spacing changes user outcomes.

limits: Tendency from research, not a universal rule; varies by site and sector.

rules.title: Muted palette
rules.description: Reduce colour saturation for a calmer look.
rules.rationale: The 2026 study finds Chinese palettes wider, more saturated and brighter, so Western palettes are comparatively more restrained. The finding is indirect: it measures Chinese sites against Western ones, not Western palettes in absolute terms.

evidence.summary: Chinese palettes measured as more saturated and brighter, implying a comparatively more restrained Western baseline.

sources.locator: Section 2.2 other results: Chinese palettes wider, more saturated, brighter
docs/02 visual level: contained, more desaturated palettes in the West

gaps: Relative finding, no absolute Western saturation value.
Evidence comes from institutional (municipal) homepages; commercial sites are not covered.
No evidence that desaturating a site improves experience.

limits: Tendency from research, not a universal rule; varies by site and sector.
Must keep text contrast at or above WCAG AA.

history.change: Dimension and pole assigned and versioning started (B18). Content unchanged from rule set 0.3.0; earlier changes are in the git history.

rules.title: Strong visual hierarchy
rules.description: Make one primary focus per view clearer.
rules.rationale: The project synthesis describes the Western model as hierarchical with few competing elements. No measurement directly supports this: the headings measure in the 2026 study is HTML semantics, which doc 01 section 3.4 warns must not be confused with visual hierarchy. Kept as a hypothesis to test.

evidence.summary: Descriptive synthesis of the Western composition model; no direct measurement of visual hierarchy.

sources.locator: Section 3.1: header, hero, hierarchical sections, few competing elements
Section 2.2: HTML headings 28.95 vs 3.52 per 1,000 text units (semantic, not visual)

gaps: No direct evidence on visual hierarchy.
HTML heading counts are a semantic measure and cannot be read as visual hierarchy.
evidence.validationPlan: Compare before/after screenshots on the Western test sites and check that the main task is found faster in internal review; add real-user test later.

limits: Tendency from research, not a universal rule; varies by site and sector.

history.change: Dimension and pole assigned and versioning started (B18). Content unchanged from rule set 0.3.0; earlier changes are in the git history.

rules.title: Quieter promotions
rules.rationale: Doc 01 section 3.3 contrasts selective Western banners with numerous Chinese ones, and the 2026 study finds fewer posters and infographics on Western homepages (66 vs 99). Reducing prominence moves toward the selective convention.

evidence.summary: Fewer posters/infographics measured on Western homepages; banners described as selective.

sources.supports: Fewer promotional-style visuals in the West

sources.locator: Section 3.3 table: banners selective vs numerous and dynamic

gaps: Evidence comes from institutional (municipal) homepages; commercial sites are not covered.
Posters and infographics are not the same as commercial promotion banners.
evidence.validationPlan: Internal before/after review (B8) on the paired test sites; add real-user testing after V1.

limits: Tendency from research, not a universal rule; varies by site and sector.

rules.title: Quieter carousels
rules.rationale: The 2026 study counts autoplay elements on 39 vs 99 homepages (West vs China). Autoplay is a proxy for carousels and banners, so the support is partial.

evidence.summary: Autoplay elements measured on fewer Western homepages.

sources.locator: Section 2.2 other results: autoplay elements 99 vs 39
sources.supports: Fewer autoplaying elements in the West

gaps: Autoplay is a proxy, not a direct count of carousels.
Evidence comes from institutional (municipal) homepages; commercial sites are not covered.
evidence.validationPlan: Internal before/after review (B8) on the paired test sites; add real-user testing after V1.

limits: Tendency from research, not a universal rule; varies by site and sector.
Does not stop or alter carousel behaviour.

rules.title: Search first
rules.description: Make the search box the most prominent control on search-led pages.
rules.rationale: Observation of Google, Bing and Western ecosystems shows search as a primary, separate entry point (doc 01 section 4-5). No study tests whether emphasizing the search box helps users; this is a hypothesis drawn from observed product design.

evidence.summary: Observed product conventions of Western search-led services; no usability data.

sources.locator: Sections 4-5: Google/Bing SERP conventions; Western users spread tasks across separate services

gaps: No study cited that tests this transformation.
Observation of a few market leaders does not generalize to all Western sites.
evidence.validationPlan: Internal before/after review (B8) on the paired test sites; add real-user testing after V1.

limits: Tendency from research, not a universal rule; varies by site and sector.
Only on pages where a search box is detected.

history.change: Dimension and pole assigned and versioning started (B18). Content unchanged from rule set 0.3.0; earlier changes are in the git history.

rules.title: Underlined links
rules.description: Make links visibly underlined so they read as links.
rules.rationale: The literature review reports more underlined links on Western sites. Underlining is also a well-established affordance, and it keeps links identifiable without relying on colour alone.

evidence.summary: Review of 17 studies reports more underlined links on Western sites.

sources.locator: Section 2.1: Western sites have more underlined links
sources.supports: Underlined links more frequent in the West

gaps: Frequency of a design choice, not evidence that it improves usability for a given user.
Methods differ across the reviewed studies.

limits: Tendency from research, not a universal rule; varies by site and sector.
Must not underline buttons or navigation chrome.

history.change: Dimension and pole assigned and versioning started (B18). Content unchanged from rule set 0.3.0; earlier changes are in the git history.

rules.title: Collapse sidebar
rules.description: Collapse secondary sidebar blocks to focus on main content.
rules.rationale: The 2026 study finds fewer peripheral blocks on Western homepages (0.61 vs 1.61). Applying this to article pages is an extrapolation, so the rule is a hypothesis.

evidence.summary: Fewer peripheral blocks measured on Western homepages; article-page use is untested.

sources.supports: Fewer peripheral blocks in the West

gaps: Evidence comes from institutional (municipal) homepages; commercial sites are not covered.
Article pages are not covered by the evidence.
Hiding content may remove useful navigation.
evidence.validationPlan: Verify in B6 that sidebar content stays reachable and that the main content is not harmed; internal review on the Western test sites.
